market_context: United States/general English; USDA raw/cooked spinach composition
title: Raw vs. cooked spinach: nutrients and differences

seo.title: Raw vs. cooked spinach: nutrition compared
seo.meta_description: Cooking collapses spinach volume and concentrates minerals per 100 g, while vitamin C and folate can decline. Boiling can also remove some soluble oxalate.
seo.search_intent: Compare raw and cooked spinach and understand why nutrient numbers change so much.

excerpt: The biggest difference between raw and cooked spinach is volume. One hundred grams raw is a large bowl; 100 g cooked is compact. Iron and calcium therefore look higher per 100 g after cooking, while vitamin C and folate can fall with heat and water. Boiling can also remove some soluble oxalate into the cooking water.
content_html:
A bowl overflowing with raw spinach can collapse into a few spoonfuls after cooking. That change in volume explains much of what looks dramatic in a 100-gram nutrition table.

Approx. per 100 gRawBoiled/drained
Iron~2.7 mg~3.5–3.7 mg
Calcium~100 mg~130–140 mg
Vitamin C~28 mg~10 mg
Fiber~2.2 g~2.4 g

Cooking did not create iron. Water balance, volume and the specific samples used in food databases explain much of the concentration change.

A cooked serving contains far more leaves

Thirty grams of raw spinach supplies only around 0.8 mg iron. A 180 g cooked portion can exceed 6 mg because that serving represents a much larger quantity of collapsed leaves.

Sensitive vitamins pay a heat cost

Vitamin C and folate can be degraded or lost into cooking water. Boiling and draining generally loses more water-soluble nutrients than methods using less water.

Oxalate matters especially for calcium

Spinach is high in oxalate, which binds calcium and sharply reduces its absorption; NIH estimates that only about 5% of spinach calcium is absorbed. Boiling can move some soluble oxalate into discarded cooking water. Iron is a separate issue: spinach iron is nonheme and its absorption depends on the meal matrix, but oxalate itself does not appear to be an important inhibitor of nonheme iron absorption in humans.

The takeaway

Raw spinach better preserves some sensitive vitamins and adds volume; cooked spinach lets you eat much more leaf in a compact serving. Both are useful, and serving weight plus mineral bioavailability explain much of the practical difference.

faq.question: Why does cooked spinach have more iron per 100 g?
faq.answer: Mostly because water, volume and concentration change. Cooking does not create iron.

faq.question: Does cooking spinach reduce oxalate?
faq.answer: Boiling can move some soluble oxalate into the cooking water, which is then discarded.
